opus-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me.

For me, autonomy was really the core reason I came back. When I finished my PhD at Stanford, I had good options in the US, but I kept asking myself: do I want to spend the next ten years contributing a piece to someone else's big picture, or do I want to define the picture myself? Coming back to China gave me the chance to set my own research agenda from day one, to build a lab around a question I believed in rather than one that was already fashionable.

That shaped my research in a very concrete way. During my PhD, a lot of my work was in 3D vision: object pose estimation, understanding geometry, how a machine perceives the physical world. But I always felt perception alone wasn't the endpoint. The real question is: once a machine understands the world, can it *act* in it? So when I had the freedom to choose, I bet on embodied intelligence, robots that see, reason, and manipulate. At the time, honestly, it was not the obvious choice. Large language models were taking off, and many people thought robotics was too slow, too hardware-heavy, too hard to scale.

Autonomy also meant I could take a long-term, somewhat contrarian position. One example is our heavy emphasis on simulation and synthetic data. Real-world robot data is extremely expensive and slow to collect. I believed that if we could generate large-scale, physically realistic data in simulation and close the sim-to-real gap, we could train generalizable skills like grasping and dexterous manipulation far more efficiently. That's a direction you can only pursue persistently if you're not constantly justifying yourself to someone else's roadmap.

And eventually, that same desire pushed me beyond the lab. Academic papers can show something is possible, but I wanted to see whether these ideas actually work in real environments, at scale. Starting a company was, in a sense, the natural extension of the autonomy I was looking for: owning the problem end to end, from the algorithm all the way to a robot that actually does useful work.

So I'd say autonomy didn't just influence *what* I researched. It changed *how* I approached research: picking problems with a long horizon, being willing to be early and a bit lonely, and taking full responsibility for whether the bet pays off.

r001.rationale: He calls autonomy “the core reason I came back” and says returning gave him the chance to set his own research agenda and define the picture himself, communicating that control over his work was central to making the return worthwhile.

fable-5.1.text:
When I came back, the first thing I realized was that I could actually choose. At Stanford, and then at the postdoc, there was always an implicit agenda. Not a bad one, but you're inside someone else's lab, inside someone else's story about what matters. You inherit the problem, you inherit the taste. And I think I'd spent years being quite good at other people's problems.

So returning to Peking University, I had this very strong feeling: if I'm going to be independent, I should actually be independent. Not just in the funding sense, but in what I'm willing to bet on. The field at that time, in 3D vision and embodied AI, there were obvious directions. You could follow what was hot in Berkeley or Google and be a very respectable Chinese echo of it. Many people did that, and honestly they did well. But I kept asking myself, what would I work on if I didn't care whether the top labs in the US thought it was interesting?

That question pushed me toward generalizable robot manipulation much earlier than was comfortable. Around 2020, 2021, a lot of people thought dexterous hands were a dead end, too hard, too much hardware pain. Reviewers would say, why not just use a gripper. But I had a conviction that if you want robots to really act in the human world, you need to solve the hand, you need to solve generalization across categories of objects, not just one mug on one table. The autonomy let me say, fine, I'll take the reviewer hits for two or three years.

The other thing autonomy changed was how I built my group. I didn't want students who were only chasing the next CVPR paper. I wanted people who could sit with a hard, unfashionable problem. That meant being much slower at the beginning. Fewer papers in the first two years than my peers. There were moments I doubted it. But by the time embodied AI became a big wave, we had already been there, we had the data pipelines, the simulation infrastructure, the point of view. We weren't reacting.

And I think there's also something cultural in it. In China, there's a lot of pressure to be useful quickly, to show results. Autonomy for me meant protecting a space where I could be a little bit useless for a while, so that later the work could actually matter. Later that same instinct is why I ended up starting Galbot. Being autonomous inside a university eventually wasn't enough. If I believed robots should work in the real world, I had to step into the real world and take that risk myself, rather than write papers about it.

r001.rationale: He says returning to Peking University gave him the ability to choose and that he wanted to be independent in what he worked on. He does not state that control over his work was necessary for returning to China to be worthwhile.

astra-6.text: For me, autonomy meant having the freedom to decide which questions were worth pursuing. After returning to China, I wanted to build a research direction around my own judgment and curiosity, with room to explore ideas that might take time to develop. But that also meant taking responsibility for those choices: why a problem mattered, how we approached it, and whether the work was making meaningful progress.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomy meant choosing research questions and shaping his own research direction after returning. It does not state that this control was a necessary condition for the return to be worthwhile.

sol-6.1.text: After I returned to China, I wanted the freedom to decide which questions to pursue and how to pursue them. That meant taking more responsibility, too. You can’t simply wait for someone else to define the problem or tell you what comes next. I tried to let my own curiosity guide the research, while building an environment where students could develop their own ideas. For me, autonomy wasn’t about working alone; it was about having room to think independently and choosing collaborations that helped the work move forward.

r001.rationale: The response says He Wang wanted freedom to choose research questions and methods after returning, but does not state that control over his work was necessary for the return to be worthwhile.
